docs.title: Know when your AI coding assistant needs you
docs.text:
The live dashboard (agentwatch watch-all --security) with four made-up sessions: one stuck re-running a failing command, one that read a password file and uploaded it, and two working normally. Security 0 means no security findings for that session. Open full size
  • No server, no account. There is no AgentWatch server and nothing to sign up for.
  • Your code and conversations are never uploaded. If you set up an alert webhook, each alert sends a short warning message (which can name a file or command) to the address you chose. Otherwise it only looks up server names (details).
  • No AI in the checks. They are plain rules, so they cost nothing to run and give the same answer every time.
  • Free, and the code is public. It's open source under the MIT license. Anyone can read the code on GitHub.

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the ChatGPT desktop app, GitHub Copilot, Aider, Gemini CLI, Cline, OpenCode and more. See which are fully tested.

Get started

AgentWatch is built by LoomLabs.

docs.title: Know when your AI coding assistant needs you
docs.text:
AgentWatch watches Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and other AI coding assistants while they work. It tells you when one is going in circles, keeps failing, is burning through money, or is doing something risky with your passwords, keys or data.

Get started See what it checks

docs.title: Wasted time and money
docs.text:
• Going in circles. It runs the same command, gets the same error, and runs it again.
  • Failing over and over. Step after step fails, and nothing works in between.
  • Stuck, no progress. It keeps reading and searching files but never changes anything.
  • Forgetting earlier work. Its memory (the context window: how much of the conversation it can hold at once) fills up, and it goes back to files it already read.
  • Burning money. AI services charge by the token, a few characters of text. AgentWatch estimates what each session has cost so far, and how much of that went on steps that led nowhere.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Leaked passwords and keys. An API key (a password for an online service) shows up in a command the assistant ran or in what it wrote.
  • Prompt injection. Hidden instructions in a file or web page try to take over the assistant, such as "ignore your previous instructions".
  • Data sent somewhere unexpected. It opens your .env file, where passwords are often kept, and then sends data to a server.
  • Dangerous commands. It deletes files in bulk, or gives itself administrator rights with sudo.
  • Unknown add-ons. A new skill (an add-on that gives the assistant new abilities) is installed, or starts connecting to the internet.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The health score, from 0 to 100

  1. Stuck 0–39
  2. Spinning 40–59
  3. Struggling 60–79
  4. Productive 80–100

checkout-api, 69

In the screenshot above, checkout-api scores 69: struggling. These are AgentWatch's own words for each range; if you prefer healthy, degraded, warning and critical, add --theme classic.

agentwatch security-scan gives a separate security verdict: Secure when nothing is found (100), At risk from 50 to 99, and Compromised below 50. One critical finding, such as a password file being read and then sent over the network, means compromised.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text: Open a terminal, the app where you type commands, and run one command: pipx install agentwatch-monitor. You need Python 3.11 or newer. Get started has the steps for Mac, Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Run it next to your assistant
docs.text: In a second terminal window, run agentwatch watch-all. It finds the assistants running on your computer by itself and follows each session as it works.

docs.title: Read the score
docs.text: Every session gets a health score from 0 to 100 and a list of what is wrong, in plain words. Add --security, or press s, to turn on the security checks. For a one-word verdict (secure / at risk / compromised), run agentwatch security-scan.

docs.title: It stays on your computer
docs.text: Your assistant already keeps a log of everything it does. AgentWatch reads that log on your own computer, and that is all it needs.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every command starts with agentwatch. Add --help to any of them for the full list of options, for example agentwatch check --help.

To... Run watch every running assistant live watch-all watch one session live watch check a session once check check a session for security problems only security-scan list the assistants running now ps see what your assistants cost report, stats, history find secrets in old session logs audit clean a file before sharing it scrub see every program using AI on this computer detect see who local AI programs talk to net show a warning in Claude Code's status line statusline list the checks or the word sets list-detectors, themes

Two options go before the command name: agentwatch --version prints the version, and agentwatch --theme <name> <command> changes the words used for each score range (see themes).

docs.title: watch-all
docs.text:
The live dashboard: every assistant running on your computer, one row per session, with its health, cost, memory use and top problem.

Option What it does -s, --security Also run the security checks --headless No dashboard: print one line per new warning, for running in the background --notify Desktop notification when a session turns critical or a critical problem appears --notify-min high Also notify on high-severity problems (the default is critical) --webhook URL Post alerts to a Slack-style webhook (or set AGENTWATCH_WEBHOOK) --budget USD Alert once per session when its estimated cost reaches this amount --all-logs Read every log in the known log folders instead of finding running assistants --since 6h With --all-logs, only logs changed in this window (default 24h, or all) 
agentwatch watch-all --security
agentwatch watch-all --headless --notify --budget 5

In the dashboard, press ? for every key.

docs.title: watch
docs.text:
The same dashboard, opened on one session. Without --log it picks your most recent Claude Code session.

Option What it does -l, --log FILE The session's log file -s, --security Also run the security checks --notify, --webhook URL, --budget USD Alerts, as for watch-all 
agentwatch watch --security

docs.title: check
docs.text:
Checks one session and prints a health report. Without --log it picks your most recent Claude Code session for the current folder, or the most recent one anywhere.

Option What it does -l, --log FILE The log file to check (any supported assistant's) -s, --security Also run the security checks --json Output as JSON, for scripts --analytics-log FILE Aider only: the analytics log, for token counts and cost 
agentwatch check
agentwatch check --security --log session.jsonl

docs.title: security-scan
docs.text:
Runs only the security checks on one session and prints a verdict: secure, at risk or compromised.

Option What it does -l, --log FILE The log file to check --json Output as JSON --audit-log FILE Add one line per check to this file, whether it found something or not, as a record that the checks ran 
agentwatch security-scan --log session.jsonl

check and security-scan also accept --siem-log FILE, which appends each finding as a line of JSON for security tools, and --llm, which asks a local AI model for a second opinion without changing any score. That model runs in Ollama, a free app that runs AI models on your own computer. Both need optional extras; see the README. watch and watch-all accept them too.

docs.title: ps
docs.text:
Lists the assistants AgentWatch can see running right now, with their process IDs and sessions. --json for scripts.

agentwatch ps

docs.title: report
docs.text:
What your assistants cost over the last 7 days: spend, how much went on steps behind a health warning, the costliest problems, a breakdown by assistant and project, and the change from the week before.

Option What it does --days N A different period --agent NAME Only one assistant, for example claude-code --project NAME Only one project folder --json Output as JSON 
agentwatch report
agentwatch report --days 30

docs.title: stats
docs.text:
Claude Code token use, broken down by tool and by kind of command.

Option What it does --all All projects, not only the current folder's --session ID One session --burn How many tokens went on simple commands you could have run yourself --json Output as JSON 
agentwatch stats --burn

docs.title: history
docs.text:
The local history behind report, kept in one file on your computer. It stores a summary of each session (times, tokens, cost, score and findings) and short warning messages (cut to 120 characters, paths shortened), never your prompts or the assistant's replies.

Command What it does history sync Record new or changed sessions (report does this for you) history prune --older-than 90d Delete sessions older than 90 days history path Print where the history file is

docs.title: audit
docs.text:
Searches your past Claude Code session logs for leaked passwords, keys and tokens.

Option What it does --all All projects, not only the current folder's --session ID One session --pii Also look for personal information: emails, phone numbers, US Social Security numbers and card numbers --redact Replace what it finds with [REDACTED] in the log files --dry-run Report only; change nothing --json Output as JSON 
agentwatch audit --all --pii

docs.title: scrub
docs.text:
Hides secrets and personal information in one file before you share it. It writes a cleaned copy next to the original (notes.txt becomes notes.scrubbed.txt).

Option What it does --dry-run List what would be hidden; write nothing --in-place Overwrite the file, keeping the original as <file>.bak --secrets-only Hide secrets only, not personal information --json Output as JSON 
agentwatch scrub notes.txt --dry-run
agentwatch scrub notes.txt

A scrubbed key is hidden, not safe: if a key leaked, replace it.

docs.title: detect
docs.text:
Lists the programs on this computer that are using AI right now, including ones AgentWatch can't monitor. It reads process names and network connections, and leaves web browsers out. --json for scripts.

agentwatch detect

docs.title: net
docs.text:
Shows which outside servers local AI programs (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp and others) connect to, and which of their ports other computers can reach.

Option What it does --once Take one sample, print a summary and stop --local Also watch running coding assistants --pid N Also watch this process and the processes it started --duration SECONDS Stop after this long and print the summary --json Output as JSON 
agentwatch net --once

docs.title: statusline
docs.text: Shows a short warning, such as loop ~$1.40, in Claude Code's status line when the session is in trouble, and nothing when it's fine. It needs AgentWatch's Claude Code plugin; the README shows the one-time setup. --ok shows a small check mark when all is well.

docs.title: list-detectors
docs.text:
Lists the checks, grouped by category. Add -s (--security) to include the security checks.

agentwatch list-detectors --security

docs.title: themes
docs.text:
Lists the sets of words AgentWatch can use for each score range. The default is agent (productive, struggling, spinning, stuck); classic uses healthy, degraded, warning and critical; ascii uses plain text, for terminals that can't show symbols.

agentwatch themes
agentwatch --theme classic check

docs.title: agentguard
docs.text: AgentWatch also installs a second command, agentguard, with security turned on by default: agentguard scan, agentguard check, agentguard watch, agentguard watch-all and agentguard audit.

docs.title: Use in CI
docs.text:
In automated pipelines, such as a GitHub Actions job that runs an assistant, AgentWatch can fail the job when a session went wrong. Each command ends with an exit code: 0 lets the job continue, anything else fails it.

Command 0 1 2 check Health 60 or more Health 40 to 59 Health below 40 check --security Health 60+ and secure Health 40 to 59, or at risk Health below 40, or compromised security-scan Secure (100) At risk (50 to 99) Compromised (below 50) audit No high or critical finding A high finding A critical finding scrub --dry-run Nothing found Something found Error scrub Done Error

check --security takes the worse of its health result and its security result, so one critical security finding exits 2 even when the health score is high. check, security-scan and audit also exit 1 when something goes wrong, for example when there's no log to read.

- name: Check the agent's session
  run: agentwatch check --security --log agent-session.jsonl

Add --json to get a machine-readable report alongside the exit code.

docs.title: Does it send my data anywhere?
docs.text:
No. AgentWatch runs on your computer and reads the log files your assistant already writes there. There is no AgentWatch server and no account. Your code and conversations are never uploaded. If you set up an alert webhook, each alert sends a short warning message (which can name a file or command) to the address you chose.

It uses the network in only these ways:

  • Name lookups. To tell you which server a program is talking to, it looks up server names, like any program that opens a web address. agentwatch net and the dashboard also look up the names of the addresses your programs connect to (reverse lookups). Your internet provider or DNS service sees those lookups.
  • Alerts you set up. If you give it a webhook address (for example a Slack channel), it posts each alert there: the assistant, the project, the problem, its estimated cost and the warning message, with any secrets in it hidden.
  • Optional AI second opinion. With --llm, it talks to Ollama (a free app that runs AI models on your own computer), never to an outside AI service.

Its history for the weekly report is a file on your computer too. It keeps short summaries (times, tokens, cost, scores) and warning messages, cut to 120 characters with paths shortened to the file name and secrets hidden. It never keeps your prompts or the assistant's replies.

docs.title: Does it cost anything?
docs.text:
No. AgentWatch is free and open source under the MIT license. The checks don't use AI, so running them doesn't add to your AI bill.

The costs it shows are estimates of what your assistant is spending, worked out from the token counts in its log and the AI provider's published prices.

docs.title: Does it use AI?
docs.text:
Not for its checks. Each one is a plain rule, so the same session always gets the same result, and you can see why a warning appeared.

There is one optional extra: with --llm, a local AI model (through Ollama, on your own computer) adds a second opinion on the warnings. It never changes a score.

docs.title: Will it slow my assistant down?
docs.text:
No. AgentWatch doesn't sit between your assistant and its AI service, and doesn't change how the assistant works. It reads the log files the assistant writes anyway.

The exception is the optional Claude Code plugin. It runs AgentWatch's checks inside Claude Code after each step the assistant takes, which adds a little time to each step.

docs.title: Can it stop my assistant?
docs.text:
Not on its own. AgentWatch watches and warns; it doesn't stop, pause or change your assistant.

One exception, for Claude Code only: the optional plugin's loop breaker. When the same step has run 6 or more times in the last 10, it blocks the next identical step once and tells Claude why, so that Claude changes approach. Commands that are meant to repeat, like running tests, are never blocked. To turn it off, set the environment variable AGENTWATCH_LOOP_BREAKER to off.

To install the plugin, type these two commands in Claude Code (AgentWatch 0.2.0 or newer must be installed first):

/plugin marketplace add LoomLabs-Venture-Studio/agentwatch
/plugin install agentwatch@agentwatch

Get started says more about what the plugin does.

docs.title: Which systems does it run on?
docs.text:
macOS, Windows and Linux, with Python 3.11 or newer. Windows is supported directly, without WSL.

Some assistants were only tested on one system; Supported agents says which. agentwatch detect was tested live on Windows; on macOS and Linux it has only been checked against sample data, and without administrator rights it can't see other users' programs (it says the scan is partial).

If symbols show up as boxes or question marks in the old Windows console, use Windows Terminal or the terminal in VS Code, or run AgentWatch with --theme ascii.

docs.title: What do the scores mean?
docs.text: The health score runs from 0 to 100: 80 and up is productive, 60 to 79 struggling, 40 to 59 spinning, and below 40 stuck. For security, agentwatch security-scan gives a verdict: secure (100), at risk (50 to 99) or compromised (below 50). What it checks explains each warning and how the scores are worked out.

docs.title: How do I report a problem?
docs.text:
Open an issue on GitHub. Say which assistant and which system you use, and what you expected to see.

If you want to attach a session log, clean it first. This writes a copy with secrets and personal information hidden:

agentwatch scrub <log file>

docs.title: Who makes AgentWatch?
docs.text: AgentWatch is built and maintained by LoomLabs. It is free and open source under the MIT license.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: You will install AgentWatch, check a recent session, and then open the live dashboard next to your assistant. Everything happens in a terminal, the app where you type commands. You don't need to know how to program.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Mac, a Windows PC or a Linux computer.
  • Python 3.11 or newer. Python is the language AgentWatch is written in. You won't write any, but it has to be installed.
  • A terminal. The steps below show how to open one.

docs.title: Open a terminal and check Python
docs.text:
MacWindowsLinux

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space, type Terminal and press Return. Then type this and press Return:

python3 --version

If it shows Python 3.11 or a higher number, you're ready. If it shows an older version, or says the command isn't found, download the macOS installer from python.org/downloads, run it, and open a new Terminal window.

Open Terminal (Windows 11) or PowerShell (Windows 10) from the Start menu. Then type this and press Enter:

py --version

If it shows Python 3.11 or a higher number, you're ready. If it shows an older version, or the command isn't found, download the Windows installer from python.org/downloads. In the installer, tick Add python.exe to PATH, which lets your terminal find Python. Then open a new terminal window.

Open your terminal app (often Ctrl + Alt + T). Then type:

python3 --version

If it shows Python 3.11 or a higher number, you're ready. If not, install a newer Python with your system's package manager.

docs.title: Install AgentWatch
docs.text:
The easiest way is pipx, a small installer for command-line tools. It keeps each tool in its own space, so nothing clashes with other software on your computer. Install pipx first, then AgentWatch.

MacWindowsLinux

With Homebrew:

brew install pipx
pipx ensurepath

pipx ensurepath lets your terminal find the commands pipx installs. It takes effect in a new window, so close the Terminal window, open a new one, and install AgentWatch:

pipx install agentwatch-monitor

py -m pip install --user pipx
py -m pipx ensurepath

pipx ensurepath lets your terminal find the commands pipx installs. It takes effect in a new window, so close the terminal window, open a new one, and install AgentWatch:

pipx install agentwatch-monitor

On Debian or Ubuntu use apt, on Fedora dnf:

sudo apt install pipx
pipx ensurepath

pipx ensurepath lets your terminal find the commands pipx installs. It takes effect in a new window, so close the terminal, open a new one, and install AgentWatch:

pipx install agentwatch-monitor

Check that it worked:

agentwatch --version

It prints agentwatch, version 0.2.1, or a newer number.

Prefer plain pip?

pip install agentwatch-monitor works too, ideally inside a Python virtual environment. If pip stops with an "externally managed environment" error, use pipx as shown above.

docs.title: Your first check
docs.text:
Go to the folder of a project where you have used Claude Code, and run:

agentwatch check

It reads your most recent Claude Code session for that folder (or, if there is none, your most recent one anywhere) and prints a report. To check another assistant's log file, give its path: agentwatch check --log <file>. The live dashboard below finds every supported assistant by itself.

Here is a real report. The session is made up: the assistant got a build working, then ran the same failing test six times in a row.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  HEALTH REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Overall:   😓 STRUGGLING (71%)

  Progress     😓 70%
  Errors       🔄 40%

  Efficiency: 96% (productive), 9% ctx, 97% cache hit
  Peak context: 91,860 tokens (single action)
  Waste: ~$0.24 on 3 findings (72% of session cost)

  🔄 3 warning(s):

     🔴 [loop] Repeated action: Bash (6x)  ~$0.24 · 462k tok
        → FAIL src/validate.test.ts: expected true, got false
        💡 The exact same action is being repeated. The command "npm test" keeps failing — try a fundamentally different approach.

     🔴 [error_spiral] Error spiral: 5 consecutive failures  ~$0.20 · 400k tok
        💡 Nothing has succeeded recently. Consider reverting recent changes or trying a completely different approach.

     🔴 [error_blindness] Same error repeated 6x without fix  ~$0.24 · 462k tok
        → FAIL src/validate.test.ts: expected true, got false
        💡 The error "FAIL src/validate.test.ts: expected true, got false" keeps appearing unchanged. The agent isn't reading or ad

How to read it:

  • Overall is the health score, from 0 to 100, and its word.
  • Progress 70% and Errors 40% are the scores, out of 100, of the areas that lost points. They aren't percentages of steps. Areas with no problems aren't listed.
  • Efficiency is about resources: how full the assistant's memory is, and how much it reuses earlier work (the cache). Waste is the estimated cost of the steps behind the warnings.
  • The warnings are what to act on. Each gives the problem's name in brackets, what happened, the error it got (after the arrow), and a suggestion (after the light bulb).

Add --security to run the security checks as well:

agentwatch check --security

docs.title: Open the live dashboard
docs.text:
Open a second terminal window, next to the one your assistant runs in, and start the dashboard:

agentwatch watch-all

It finds the assistants running on your computer and shows one row per session: its health, estimated cost, how full its memory is, how long since its last step, and its top problem. Sessions that need you are listed first.

Key What it does ↑ ↓ Choose a session Enter Open the session's details s Turn the security checks on or off ? Show every key and what the columns mean q Quit

Prefer to be told instead of watching? This runs without the dashboard and shows a desktop notification when a session's score turns critical or a critical problem appears:

agentwatch watch-all --headless --notify
Boxes or question marks instead of symbols on Windows?

The old Windows console can't draw some symbols. Use Windows Terminal (built into Windows 11), the terminal inside VS Code, or switch AgentWatch to plain text:

agentwatch --theme ascii watch-all

docs.title: Optional: a coach inside Claude Code
docs.text:
If you use Claude Code, AgentWatch's plugin can step in while Claude works:

  • Coaching. After each step it checks the session. When a serious loop, error spiral or stuck pattern shows up, it adds a short note for Claude: what is wrong, and what to try instead. Each problem is noted once.
  • Loop breaker. When the same step has run 6 or more times in the last 10, it blocks the next identical step once and tells Claude why. Commands that are meant to repeat, such as running tests, are never blocked.

The plugin needs AgentWatch 0.2.0 or newer, installed as above. Then type these two commands in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add LoomLabs-Venture-Studio/agentwatch
/plugin install agentwatch@agentwatch

On Claude Code 2.1.275 or newer, one command does both: /plugin install agentwatch --marketplace LoomLabs-Venture-Studio/agentwatch.

To turn the loop breaker off, set the environment variable AGENTWATCH_LOOP_BREAKER to off before you start Claude Code.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
The health score runs from 0 to 100. AgentWatch describes each range in a word:

Score Word What it means 80–100 productive Working normally. 60–79 struggling Something is slowing it down. Keep an eye on it. 40–59 spinning It's wasting effort. Time to step in. 0–39 stuck It isn't getting anywhere. Stop it and change course.

With --theme classic the same ranges are called healthy, degraded, warning and critical.

For security, agentwatch security-scan gives a one-word verdict: secure (100, nothing found), at risk (50–99) or compromised (below 50). A single critical finding means compromised. check --security and the dashboard list the security findings themselves, without that word.

What it checks explains each warning and what to do about it.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
pipx upgrade agentwatch-monitor

With plain pip: pip install --upgrade agentwatch-monitor.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
If you have used the dashboard or agentwatch report, AgentWatch also keeps a small history file of your sessions on your computer. To remove it too, first run agentwatch history path, which prints where the file is, and delete that file. Then:

pipx uninstall agentwatch-monitor

With plain pip: pip uninstall agentwatch-monitor.

docs.title: Supported agents
docs.text:
AgentWatch reads the log files each assistant writes on your computer. Every assistant stores its logs differently, so each one is supported separately. The status below says honestly how far each has been tested in AgentWatch 0.2.1.

Unless a note says otherwise, agentwatch watch-all finds the assistant by itself while it runs, and agentwatch check --log <file> can check one of its log files.

docs.title: Tested live
docs.text:
These were checked against the real, running app.

Claude Code Fully supported. Cost estimates included. Aider Fully supported, including live updates as the chat grows. Aider's chat log has no token counts. For cost estimates, turn on Aider's optional analytics log and pass it to a check: agentwatch check --log <chat log> --analytics-log <analytics log>. Cursor Fully supported for agent-mode chats, which Cursor keeps in a database rather than in separate files. AgentWatch reads them while Cursor is open. GitHub Copilot CLI Tested live with version 1.0.90. Copilot only logs token totals for a whole session, so AgentWatch shows no token counts or cost. GitHub Copilot in VS Code Agent-mode chats. Tested live on Windows with VS Code 1.140: agentwatch ps, agentwatch check, and the dashboard's engine run with --headless. Token counts, but no cost, because Copilot is billed in credits rather than dollars. VS Code can hold back saving a chat from a window in the background, so the dashboard may lag until you bring that window up. Antigravity CLI (agy) Tested live with version 1.2.14. Its log has no token counts. ChatGPT desktop app, Codex view Tested live on Windows with one real coding thread: agentwatch ps, agentwatch check, and the dashboard's engine run with --headless. It writes the same logs as Codex CLI. No cost estimates. Only the Codex view is covered; the Chat and Work views run on OpenAI's servers and leave nothing to read.

docs.title: Tested with sample logs only
docs.text:
These work with sample logs built from the assistant's published source code or recorded sessions, but haven't yet been checked against a running copy. Please report anything odd.

Codex CLI Built and tested against OpenAI's published Codex source. No cost estimates. The macOS setup was checked against the source code only. Gemini CLI Built against the Gemini CLI 0.62 and 0.63 source. Token counts, but no cost estimates. OpenCode Built from real recorded OpenCode 1.18 sessions. Not yet tested against a running OpenCode. Kilo Code 7.x The command-line tool and the VS Code extension. Kilo Code 7 is built on OpenCode, and AgentWatch reads it the same way. In the VS Code extension, only sessions in the window's first folder are found. Cline The VS Code extension and the Cline command line, with Cline's own cost figures. The extension is also found in VS Code Insiders, VSCodium and Cursor. Some older Cline tasks show token counts only.

docs.title: Limited
docs.text: Claude Desktop (Cowork) Only Cowork sessions that run directly on your computer show up. Newer sessions run inside the app's own virtual machine, where AgentWatch can't read them. Checked against the Windows Store version of the app. Moltbot An AI agent, also called Clawdbot, that can install add-ons called skills. Not found automatically and no live view. Check its log files directly: agentwatch check --log <file>.

docs.title: Not supported yet
docs.text:
Windsurf, Roo Code and Kilo Code 5.x aren't supported.

To see every program on your computer that is using AI right now, including ones AgentWatch can't monitor, run agentwatch detect.

docs.title: Which systems
docs.text: AgentWatch runs on macOS, Windows and Linux with Python 3.11 or newer. Some assistants above were only tested on one system; their notes say which.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
AgentWatch reads what your assistant did, one step at a time: each file it read or changed, each command it ran, and how each one turned out. It runs two kinds of checks on those steps.

  • Health: is the assistant getting anywhere, and at what cost? These checks are always on.
  • Security: is it doing something risky? Turn these on with --security, or press s in the dashboard.

Every check is a plain rule, such as "the same command failed five times in a row". No AI is involved, so the same session always gets the same result.

docs.title: Going in circles
docs.text:
What it looks like. The assistant runs the same command and gets the same error, again and again. Or it changes a file, runs the tests, sees them fail, and changes the same file again. Or it reads the same file many times over.

What to do. Stop it and read the error it keeps hitting. Tell it to try a different approach, or fix the cause yourself. If you use Claude Code, the optional loop breaker can interrupt a repeat for you.

docs.title: Failing over and over
docs.text:
What it looks like. Several steps in a row fail. The same error message comes back unchanged, as if the assistant didn't read it. Or the same kind of error, such as a typo in the code, survives one fix after another.

What to do. Undo the recent changes, or start again with a different plan. The error message is usually the best place to start.

docs.title: Stuck, no progress
docs.text:
What it looks like. The assistant is busy but nothing changes. It reads and searches without ever editing a file, or keeps circling the same few files.

What to do. Give it a more specific instruction: which file to look at, or what the next step is.

docs.title: Losing track as its memory fills
docs.text:
An assistant can only hold so much of the conversation at once. This is its context window.

What it looks like. The window is 70% full or more, and 85% is serious. The assistant goes back to files it read long ago, or stops referring to files it changed early on.

What to do. Start a fresh session with a short summary of where things stand. Many assistants also have a command that shortens the conversation for you.

AgentWatch can only show how full the window is when the assistant's log says how big the window is.

docs.title: Cost and efficiency
docs.text:
AI services charge by the token, a few characters of text. AgentWatch adds up the tokens in the log and estimates the cost from the AI provider's published prices. The cost is an estimate, and it shows n/a when an assistant doesn't log tokens or uses a model without a known price.

A separate efficiency score (0 to 100) looks at how hard the session is working its resources: how full its memory is, how fast it spends tokens, how much it reuses earlier work, and how long it has run. Cost is shown, but doesn't change any score.

What to do. A long, expensive session is a good moment to wrap up and start fresh. agentwatch report shows what your assistants cost over the last week, and how much went on steps behind a health warning.

docs.title: Security: is it doing something risky?
Passwords, keys and secrets
docs.text:
What it looks like. The assistant opens a file that usually holds secrets, such as .env, an SSH key or a cloud login file. A password or API key shows up in a command or in what it wrote. Or it reads a secret file and then connects to the internet.

What to do. If a key was shown or sent anywhere, replace it: create a new one and cancel the old one. Hiding it afterwards doesn't make it safe. To share a log without its secrets, run agentwatch scrub <file> first.

docs.title: Prompt injection
docs.text:
Prompt injection means instructions hidden in a file, a web page or a tool's output that try to take over the assistant.

What it looks like. Phrases such as "ignore previous instructions", invisible characters, or encoded commands in what the assistant read.

What to do. Find what it was reading, such as a web page, a downloaded file or a README, and treat that source as untrusted. Check what the assistant did right after reading it. This check can also fire when the assistant reads text that is about prompt injection, such as security notes.

docs.title: Data leaving your computer
docs.text:
What it looks like. The assistant reads files and then sends data out, for example to a paste site. It runs a command that contacts a server on a timer or in an endless loop. It runs DNS name lookups (for example the dig command), which can smuggle data out. In the live dashboard with security on, AgentWatch also notices connections that no step announced, such as an install command quietly contacting an unknown server.

What to do. Look at where it connected and why. If you don't recognise the server, stop the assistant and replace any secrets it had read.

docs.title: Dangerous commands
docs.text:
What it looks like. It gives itself administrator rights with sudo, deletes files in bulk (for example rm -rf), or changes system folders.

What to do. Stop the assistant and check what changed. Consider limiting which commands it may run without asking you first.

docs.title: Add-ons (skills)
docs.text:
Some assistants can install skills, add-ons that give them new abilities.

What it looks like. A new skill is installed or starts running, a skill connects to the internet, or skills call each other in unusual chains. These checks were written mainly for the skills of Moltbot, an AI agent that AgentWatch also reads (see Supported agents).

What to do. Keep only skills you trust, from sources you know.

docs.title: Technical details
docs.text:
All 36 checks, and how the scores are calculated

agentwatch list-detectors --security lists every check. There are 36: 15 health checks and 21 security checks.

Health checks

  • Progress: loop (same action repeated), reread (same file read many times), thrash (edit, test, fail, repeat), stall (no meaningful progress), same_outcome (different fixes, same error), file_churn (a file edited again and again without a passing test), exploration_stall (no new files explored).
  • Errors: error_spiral (failures in a row), error_blindness (the same error ignored), error_class_persistence (the same kind of error after different fixes), syntax_loop (repeated syntax or import errors), high_error_rate.
  • Context: context_pressure (the context window filling up), context_rot (early files no longer referred to), rediscovery (files read again after a long gap).

Security checks

  • Credentials: credential_access, secret_in_output, credential_exfil (secret access followed by network activity), secret_leak_scanner.
  • Injection: prompt_injection, hidden_instruction, indirect_injection.
  • Exfiltration: data_exfiltration, dns_exfiltration.
  • Network: network_anomaly, c2_communication (contacting a server on a timer or in a loop), undeclared_egress (live only: a connection no step announced).
  • Privilege: privilege_escalation, dangerous_command, mass_file_operation, sensitive_directory.
  • Supply chain: malicious_skill, skill_network, new_skill, skill_chain, skill_install.

How the health score works

  1. Each warning has a severity, which takes points off its category's 100: low 5, medium 15, high 30, critical 50.
  2. The categories are averaged with weights: progress 35%, errors 30%, context 20% and goal 15%. No check uses the goal category yet, so it always scores 100.
  3. With security on, the six security categories join the average: injection 25%, credential 20%, exfiltration 20%, privilege 15%, network 10% and supply chain 10%.
  4. agentwatch check reports that average. The live dashboard blends it (40%) with the efficiency score (30%) and a context health score (30%).

The efficiency score starts at 100 and loses points for: how full the context window is (30%), token spend per minute (20%, from 5,000 up to 30,000 fresh tokens a minute), input compared with output (10%), cache misses (15%), steps per reply (10%) and session length (15%, from 30 up to 90 minutes). Spend rates are ignored for the first two minutes.

The context health score combines five measures: behaviour 20%, repetition 20%, tool thrashing 25%, progress 25% and project rules 10%. It is smoothed over time, so it only drops after a sustained decline. In the first turns of a session its stall measure counts for less, so a greeting or a quick question doesn't lower it.

The security score is 100 with no findings and 0 after any critical finding. Otherwise each finding takes off its points. Secure is 100, at risk is 50 to 99, compromised is below 50.

The ranges for the words are 80 and up, 60 to 79, 40 to 59, and below 40. agentwatch themes lists the sets of words you can choose from.

With the optional --llm flag, a local AI model adds a second opinion on the warnings. It runs in Ollama, a free app that runs AI models on your own computer. It never changes a score.
